quantum-devices.title: Noise-Induced Topology in Chiral Quantum Walks
quantum-devices.summary: Noise typically destroys quantum coherence and washes out transport phenomena that rely on interference. Chiral quantum walks are a case in point: a particle hopping on a lattice threaded by a magnetic flux can spread asymmetrically due to interference between paths, an asymmetry that noise is expected to erase. Remarkably, we find that the most ubiquitous noise -- random fluctuations of on-site energies (dephasing) -- instead renders this asymmetry topologically robust. The density profile develops a skewness that grows in time while its center stays fixed, and in a finite chain the late-time relaxation modes pile up at one edge: a skin effect lacking the drift of conventional non-Hermitian skin effects. With multiple sites per unit cell, the dephasing strength alone can cause a topological phase transition, reversing the asymmetry. On a flux ladder with noisy rung hopping, the noise causes a drift of rung coherences, a quantum ratchet with no classical counterpart. Underlying these effects, the noise-averaged dynamics is an interacting (generically non-integrable) Lindbladian that remains analytically tractable. The modes governing late-time relaxation are bound states of the noise-induced interaction and form a band with a point gap, absent both without noise and under postselection, whose winding number fixes the direction of the asymmetry. These effects are within reach of several experimental platforms, including synthetic lattices, superconducting qubits, and optical lattices.

quantum-devices.title: Superconducting Qubits as Quantum Targets for Direct Particle Scattering
quantum-devices.summary: We introduce a novel approach to particle detection in which a superconducting qubit itself serves as the scattering target and a resolved transition between circuit eigenstates constitutes the observable final state. The scattering amplitude factorizes into the incident-particle current and a finite-momentum electromagnetic transition response of the qubit. This momentum dependence is essential in that the energy transfer is fixed by the microwave-scale level spacing, whereas a nonrelativistic incident particle can transfer a spatial momentum parametrically larger than that energy and thereby resolve the device geometry. For charge-dominated processes, we recast the response as an induced-offset-charge kernel obtained from an auxiliary electrostatic weighting potential, providing a practical route from circuit geometry to a differential scattering cross section. We illustrate the framework with an Xmon-style transmon and photon-mediated scattering of dark matter. The exceptionally small qubit transition threshold opens sensitivity to an eV-to-keV mass regime that is largely unexplored by existing direct-detection experiments.

quantum-devices.title: Dynamically modulated light-matter interactions for ancilla-tolerant bosonic control
quantum-devices.summary: Strong light-matter interactions are central to state-of-the-art quantum technologies, spanning platforms as diverse as Rydberg atoms, trapped ions, and superconducting circuits. In superconducting circuits, the strong dispersive coupling between microwave photons (light) and ancillary qubits (matter) has enabled universal bosonic control and quantum error correction. However, this always-on dispersive interaction propagates errors from the ancillary qubits to the bosonic systems both while idling and when performing operations, introducing a trade-off between control strength and fidelity. We break this trade-off by introducing a parametrically activated hybridization between the bosonic modes and ancilla qubits, keeping both elements decoupled when not active. When activated, this hybridization mediates a dynamic light-matter coupling with non-trivial engineered symmetries, permitting resilience to ancilla decay and dephasing. This dynamic coupling functions as a new control primitive that offers a route to bosonic processors whose performance is set by the oscillator, rather than the ancilla.

quantum-devices.title: Motional Decoherence of the internal state of an atom by vacuum and thermal fluctuations of a quantum field: Necessity of a fully relativistic treatment
quantum-devices.summary: We consider a massive object, such as a neutral atom or an Unruh-DeWitt detector, moving at constant speed in a quantum field and investigate how motion affects the quantum coherence of its internal degrees of freedom, manifesting as quantum dispersion in the absence of a quantum field, and decoherence in its presence. Our investigation aims to serve two purposes: One is to obtain the correct results for these effects, which are essential for the design of quantum information processing schemes where the quantum coherence of an atom's internal degrees of freedom is of major concern. The other is to expose the fallacies in commonplace approaches, which start with a non-relativistic calculation and then add on relativistic ``corrections". We first show a fully relativistic calculation of the internal dynamics based on covariance principles, and then one which ignores these principles, often justified by the atom's slow motion. By a direct comparison of results from these two approaches, we identify {significant discrepancies} in a non-relativistic treatment, even at low atomic speeds. The proper procedure, and a much safer one in terms of accuracy, is recommended here: first derive the dynamics and the necessary regularizations within a fully covariant relativistic framework. Only after the exact, internally consistent equations of motion are established should low-velocity limits be extracted from them. Only in this way can all the relativistic effects which matter: time dilation, aberration, non-inertial mass shifts, be systematically preserved, and accurate results obtained.

quantum-devices.title: Analog quantum simulation of paraparticle statistics
quantum-devices.summary: Bosonic and fermionic quantum statistics describe all known elementary and emergent particles in three dimensions, although many attempts have been made to discover other valid quantum statistical frameworks. One recent formulation proposes "$R$-paraparticles," indistinguishable particles with nonlocal internal degrees of freedom governed by generalized exchange rules [Wang and Hazzard, Nature 637, 314 (2025)]. Here, we emulate a species of paraparticle that exhibits a generalized Pauli exclusion principle using a superconducting qubit lattice. We confirm its unique quantum statistics by measuring a $180^\circ$ phase shift under paraparticle exchange, observing antibunching independent of internal degrees of freedom under two-particle interference at a beamsplitter, and finding a thermal occupation inconsistent with both Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics. These results demonstrate that parastatistics are observable on quantum simulation platforms, further motivating their use to explore theorized new phases of matter.

quantum-devices.title: Nonreciprocal generation of Bell states via cooperative dissipation in a qubit-magnon system
quantum-devices.summary: Directionally generating and controlling quantum states is critical in chiral quantum technologies. Here, we propose a scheme for the nonreciprocal generation of Bell states via cooperative dissipation in a qubit-magnon system, consisting of a superconducting transmon qubit and a yttrium iron garnet sphere subject to a bias magnetic field. The cooperative dissipation between them is induced by coupling both to a common transmission-line waveguide. Due to this cooperative dissipation, the system possesses a dark eigenstate within the single-excitation subspace. Under appropriate parameter conditions, the dark eigenstate reduces to a specific Bell state. With the assistance of a drive pulse, the system can be prepared in this Bell state (i.e., the dark eigenstate). In particular, we find that the dark eigenstate corresponds to different Bell states under positive ($+\mathbf{B}_0$) and negative ($-\mathbf{B}_0$) bias fields. Consequently, nonreciprocal Bell-state generation is achieved: $+\mathbf{B}_0$ yields one Bell state, while $-\mathbf{B}_0$ yields the other. Moreover, we define a fidelity-based nonreciprocal rate to quantify this nonreciprocity. Our work establishes cooperative dissipation as a versatile resource for nonreciprocal entangled-state generation, opening a promising route toward chiral quantum technologies.

quantum-devices.title: Towards Optimal Routing Strategies for qLDPC codes on Silicon Spin Qubits
quantum-devices.summary: One of the major challenges of implementing high-rate quantum error correction codes, like qLDPC codes, is realizing the required long-range interactions. Spin qubit platforms can provide this connectivity by shuttling qubits next to each other whenever they need to interact. When doing this, the performance of the code depends on the shuttling strategy. We study memory experiments of the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle (Gross) code on two shuttling grids for future spin qubit devices: a square grid and a square grid with diagonals. We compare three shuttling strategies, structured and random initial layouts, and a range of shuttling noise models spanning best- and worst-case scenarios. The best strategy minimizes the longest distance travelled rather than the total distance. The initial layout has only a weak effect, whereas adding diagonals to the grid reduces the logical error rate by up to two orders of magnitude which may have implications for future hardware design.

quantum-devices.title: All-to-All Connectivity in Superconducting Qubits via Metamaterial-Mediated Interactions
quantum-devices.summary: We show that encoding superconducting qubits as dual-rail or spin-locked transmons lets a metamaterial waveguide couple them all-to-all while suppressing the spurious entanglement that burdens shared-mode architectures, a step toward the non-local connectivity that quantum low-density parity-check codes require. In a bare-transmon architecture, the dispersive coupling between each populated mode and every idle qubit attached to it entangles spectators with the gate, and cancelling it by dynamical decoupling lengthens every gate. The encoding suppresses this coupling at the hardware level, from second to fourth order in the inverse qubit--mode detuning. A two-tone cross-resonance drive then generates a Mølmer-Sørensen interaction between encoded qubits, which we use for an entangling gate and a joint parity measurement, both selective and parallelizable through different modes. Simulating two dual-rail transmons sharing three resonators with a mode lifetime of $30\,μ$s, we find that heralding transmon relaxation as erasure leaves a gate infidelity of $1.4\times10^{-3}$ at $152$~ns, dominated by photon loss. Photon loss and mode crowding together bound the array size. The gate duration must exceed the inverse mode spacing, which shrinks as the array lengthens, while photon loss grows with gate duration. This bound grows linearly with the mode lifetime and with the inter-resonator coupling; at a lifetime of $150\,μ$s, five times the simulated value, and a coupling of $80$~MHz, a $10^{-3}$ error budget admits $13$ qubits on $25$ resonators.
quantum-devices.comment: 9 pages, 2 figures (main text with End Matter) + 23 pages of Supplemental Material

quantum-devices.title: Experimental Realization of a Nonreciprocal Quantum Battery
quantum-devices.summary: Quantum batteries promise faster and more efficient energy storage and extraction by harnessing quantum mechanics, serving as essential building blocks for future quantum devices. A key practical requirement-unidirectional energy flow during charging-is straightforward in classical batteries via potential difference, yet remains a major challenge in the quantum regime due to the inherent reciprocity of coherent coupling. Here, we realize the first backflow-free, nonreciprocal quantum battery in the few-quantum regime, implemented in a highly controlled trapped-ion system via a qubit-reservoir engineering technique. By subtly tailoring quantum interference between coherent and dissipative couplings of two laser-cooled motional modes, we achieve strictly unidirectional energy flow from the charger to the battery. We observe maximum charging power at an exceptional point and demonstrate a complete charge-discharge cycle with unitary work extraction. This work establishes the foundation for directional energy transfer and storage in micro- and nanoscale quantum devices, with broad implications for nonreciprocal energy harvesting, precision metrology, information processing, and quantum thermodynamics.

quantum-devices.title: Quantum simulation of real-time Yukawa dynamics with qubits and qumodes
quantum-devices.summary: Real-time quantum simulation of field theories offers access to scattering and decay dynamics, circumventing the limitations of Euclidean lattice methods. However, representing bosonic fields on qubits requires a finite-dimensional approximation and can entail costly multi-qubit operations. Hybrid qubit-qumode architectures avoid this by encoding bosonic fields directly in oscillators. We formulate scattering in the (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory for such a device, with staggered fermions on qubits and the scalar on qumodes. Trapped ions are a natural candidate, with the fermions on the internal states of the ions and the scalar on their collective motion, so that the Yukawa coupling becomes a native spin-dependent displacement. Emulating the device with tensor networks, we study the decay of a single scalar particle and fermion-antifermion scattering around the resonance region, using observables that can be measured on the device natively. We compare the results with those obtained using lattice perturbation theory. The emulation is able to resolve corrections beyond the Dyson summation of the one-loop self-energy.

quantum-devices.title: Topologically Protected Edge States in a Single Flux Qubit
quantum-devices.summary: We show that topological edge states can be realized in a simple superconducting circuit composed of an inductively shunted flux qubit. The Josephson potential of that qubit forms a honeycomb lattice similar to the case of graphene. The additional shunting element produces a quartic potential along one flux direction, which effectively creates a boundary in flux space. We map analytically the low-energy dynamics of the circuit to an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) chain, in which a quartic potential is added to the usual SSH Hamiltonian. This mapping is confirmed by numerical simulations of the full superconducting circuit. We argue that chiral symmetry still holds for the edge states of the extended model around a chiral point in parameter space. Close to this point, we numerically find that edge states in our superconducting circuit are topologically protected against perturbations that obey chiral symmetry, as is the case for charge noise. Our results show that topological effects previously thought to occur in multi-qubit systems, such as protection against decoherence, can also be found in much simpler single superconducting qubits.

quantum-devices.title: Control-Noise Trade-offs in Industrially Integrated ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ Spin-1/2 Qubits
quantum-devices.summary: Scaling silicon spin qubits to fault-tolerant processors requires semiconductor foundry integration, yet it remains unclear how industrial fabrication and dense device integration affect qubit control and noise. Here we study ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ electron spin-1/2 qubits fabricated using Intel's industry-compatible 300 mm process and incorporating micromagnets for electrically driven spin resonance, using a high-performance device fabricated in the RIKEN research cleanroom as a reference. Primitive $π/2$-gate fidelities reach the 99.99% level in the Intel devices, which also exhibit longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability across several measured characteristics. In the present Intel devices, the micromagnets are integrated inline with the back-end-of-line (BEOL) contact routing, with their separation from the quantum well set through the vertical stack design. Relative to the reference, their larger separation contributes to weaker longitudinal and transverse magnetic-field gradients. The weaker longitudinal gradient suppresses the conversion of charge noise into qubit-frequency fluctuations, whereas the weaker transverse gradient reduces electrically driven spin-resonance efficiency and makes drive-dependent errors relevant at lower Rabi frequencies. Additional BEOL routing and metal levels required for two-dimensional arrays make such placement decisions increasingly consequential when scaling. These results establish an integration-level control-noise trade-off linking micromagnet placement within densely routed layouts to achievable gate performance, while very high-fidelity operation remains possible in industrially fabricated devices.
quantum-devices.comment: 28 pages, 4 main figures and 5 extended data figures

quantum-devices.title: Symmetries and model reduction in a $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit
quantum-devices.summary: Engineered symmetries in superconducting circuits can protect quantum information; much like selection rules in atomic physics, they forbid transitions between the qubit states. Protected circuits, however, combine several loops and islands and host multiple nonlinearly coupled modes, calling for reduced low-energy models that inherit the circuit symmetries and make the protection manifest. We develop such a reduction for the $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit, recently realized experimentally with a two-Cooper-pair interferometer, whose circuit hosts three coupled modes. Exploiting the separation of energy scales between the heavy transmon mode and the light internal modes of the interferometer, we derive an effective single-band Born-Oppenheimer model, including its geometric correction, and extend it to several bands. We identify the symmetries of the full and reduced Hamiltonians and derive exact selection rules. Finally, we identify a parameter regime beyond the single-band description that suppresses flux-noise dephasing without degrading charge-noise protection.

quantum-devices.title: Real-time BP decoding of a high-rate QEC code
quantum-devices.summary: We present a real-time FPGA decoder for a high-rate $[[512,174,8]]$ 3D product qLDPC code. We construct a circuit-level detector-error model for a compact syndrome-extraction schedule and propose a small parallel ensemble of row-wise serial min-sum decoders with cumulative memory. The decoder matches $\text{BP+OSD-CS}_\text{10}$ accuracy with one core and Relay-BP accuracy with three cores. The FPGA implementation meets the latency budget of neutral-atom and trapped-ion systems. An ASIC implementation would improve the latency, enabling real time decoding even for superconducting systems. At a physical error rate of $p=10^{-3}$, three FPGA devices decode 174 logical qubits with a logical error rate of $5\times10^{-7}$ and effective distance 6. For $p=10^{-4}$, and assuming the number of BP iterations is capped to 30, the decoder's average latency is $5.1\,$\textmu s and its worst-case latency is $97.9\,$\textmu s.

quantum-devices.title: Vacuum amplification across a programmable bosonic Bogoliubov stability boundary in a trapped-ion chain
quantum-devices.summary: A quantum oscillator always carries vacuum fluctuations, and modulating its parameters converts them into correlated pairs of real quanta. This vacuum amplification underlies squeezed light and Hawking radiation. In a closed quadratic system, pair creation competes with the energy splitting of the modes, and growth turns exponential only once pairing overcomes the splitting. Here we realize this competition in two motional modes of a trapped-ion chain. A two-mode-squeezing drive creates the pairs, and a beam-splitter coupling splits the motion into two coupled modes at different frequencies. The two rates are tuned and calibrated independently. Starting near the motional ground state, we cross the stability boundary in two ways. First, with the drive at the sum of the two bare-mode frequencies, the phonon number stays bounded until the pairing rate exceeds the splitting and grows exponentially beyond it. Second, tuning the drive into resonance with one coupled mode lowers the threshold to zero, and only that mode is amplified into a squeezed vacuum. Separate control of the two interactions makes the threshold for vacuum amplification programmable. This control can be used to simulate particle creation and quantum phase transitions, and to operate parametrically driven bosonic devices close to their stability limit.

quantum-devices.title: Comparison of entangling strategies for unitary synthesis
quantum-devices.summary: Trapped-ion quantum computers are promising as a platform for realizing quantum computational advantage. They promise long coherence times, near all-to-all connectivity, and potential multiqubit gates as distinguishing advantages compared to competing platforms. Regarding these advantages, it is crucial to understand the trade-offs between increasing engineering complexity and actual improvements in running quantum algorithms with a more flexible gate set. In this work, we investigate this question and develop a versatile toolset to evaluate the performance of gate sets composed of native Mølmer--Sørensen multiqubit gates. To this end, we employ unitary synthesis as an application-agnostic benchmark target and identify specific hardware requirements for multiqubit gates to be advantageous.

quantum-devices.title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
quantum-devices.summary: While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among the leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy. Discussions of hardware implementations are reported alongside an initial proof-of-principle experiment on a Quantinuum System Model H2 trapped-ion quantum processor.

quantum-devices.title: High-Fidelity Universal Quantum Gates in a Cryogenic Atom Array
quantum-devices.summary: Neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays have emerged as a leading platform for quantum information processing. The fidelity of entangling gates mediated by Rydberg interactions has improved rapidly and is increasingly constrained by blackbody-radiation-induced transitions, which shorten Rydberg lifetimes and create contaminant states that can cause correlated errors. Cryogenic environments can suppress these transition rates by more than an order of magnitude. However, realizing a universal gate set in such an environment has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we demonstrate a universal quantum gate set in a cryogenic $^{133}$Cs atom array, with a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.970(2)% and a raw two-qubit entangling-gate fidelity of 99.76(8)%, within the range of leading room-temperature implementations. The entangling gate uses direct single-photon coupling between the electronic ground state and a Rydberg $P$ state, avoiding scattering and light shifts associated with two-photon coupling. The gate operates at a modest Rabi frequency of $2π\times4.3$ MHz. The measured fidelity agrees with our error model dominated by atomic motion, indicating a straightforward route to higher fidelity through improved cooling, while the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below $3\times10^{-4}$. These results establish a path to entangling-gate fidelities substantially beyond the current state of the art through cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, reducing the overhead for fault-tolerant computation.

quantum-devices.title: SeQUeNCe.DQC: Full-stack Simulation of Distributed Quantum Computing
quantum-devices.summary: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) connects multiple quantum processing units to overcome the scale limits of monolithic hardware. We introduce SeQUeNCe$.$DQC a new top-level module within the SeQUeNCe package that compiles monolithic circuits into topology-aware execution plans and coordinates their execution using SeQUeNCe's existing quantum-network modules and protocols. We validate SeQUeNCe$.$DQC by reproducing a two-node trapped-ion Grover experiment in simulation and comparing success probabilities with the reported 71% benchmark. We then evaluate how compiler strategy, topology, and memory capacity jointly govern distributed circuit execution time and success rate. In these experiments, our hybrid compilers successfully identified mixed TeleGate/TeleData execution plans that outperformed pure gate-teleportation strategies. By capturing the physical overhead of distributed quantum primitives, SeQUeNCe$.$DQC provides a rigorous platform for co-designing DQC software and hardware architectures.

quantum-devices.title: NAKO: A Benchmarking Framework for Evaluating and Diagnosing Neutral-Atom Quantum Compilers
quantum-devices.summary: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors couple gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel atom transport, so compiler decisions jointly determine physical execution costs. Evaluating these compilers requires attainable resource references and a way to trace excess costs to their causes. We present NAKO, a benchmarking framework that parameterizes circuits by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one- and two-qubit gate densities, and assigns attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers. Each benchmark is paired with an executable reference schedule; under the stated execution model, construction guarantees minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts, and minimum movement among schedules with the minimum Rydberg-stage count. Comparing compiler outputs with these references quantifies resource gaps, while reference mappings and intermediate physical states enable controlled interventions that trace excess costs to specific compiler decisions. In a 648-run evaluation of Enola and OLSQ-DPQA, NAKO identifies distinct bottlenecks. For Enola, placement scoring and cross-stage layout management contribute to excess movement; diagnosis-guided interventions reduce mean movement by 78.9% across five matched circuits. For OLSQ-DPQA, premature candidate selection and limited exploration of preparatory states produce avoidable entangling stages and routing intervals; four fixed-checkpoint continuations each eliminate one Rydberg stage and one routing interval without increasing movement. NAKO thus links resource targets backed by constructive optimality guarantees to controlled diagnosis and validation of compiler-specific resource savings.

quantum-devices.title: Individually Addressed Logical Pauli Measurements by QLDPC Surgery on a Trapped Ion Quantum Computer
quantum-devices.summary: Quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes may lead to order-of-magnitude reductions in the qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Achieving this improved overhead requires logical operations that selectively address individual logical qubits encoded within multi-qubit code blocks. Recently proposed architectures achieve this through QLDPC surgery, in which non-destructive Pauli measurements are performed using ancillary ''gadget'' systems transiently entangled with the code block, generalising lattice surgery. Here we implement QLDPC surgery on a [[10,2,3]] generalised bicycle code using Quantinuum's H2-2 trapped ion processor. A single-round surgery measurement using seven gadget qubits measures the $\bar{X}_1$ operator with a 0.72 [0.32, 1.41]% (95% credible interval) error rate and agrees with subsequent transversal measurement with 1.03 [0.60, 1.65]% error. Decoding across three rounds of syndrome extraction suppresses the gadget measurement error, reducing the error rate to below 0.26%. The syndrome after surgery confirms return to the code space and the unaddressed ''spectator'' qubit is preserved with error 0.21 [0.04, 0.67]% during the three-round measurement. We further demonstrate composition of conjugate basis gadgets by sequentially measuring $\bar{X}_1$ then $\bar{Z}_2$, reusing the gadget qubits, and obtain a 1.12 [0.60, 1.94]% error in the $\bar{Z}_2$ measurement. These results constitute a hardware validation of the generalised surgery primitive underlying Pauli-based computing for QLDPC architectures.

quantum-devices.title: Generating Multipartite Entanglement via Structured-Bath Engineering
quantum-devices.summary: We present how to dissipatively prepare genuinely multipartite-entangled steady states with mutually independent local reservoirs by harnessing an Abelian strong symmetry and temporal bath correlations. In interacting Ising chains, we demonstrate that, for a broad class of system-environment couplings, flat baths exponentially erase Ising-axis correlations. Structured baths overcome this obstruction by converting temporal bath correlations into classical spatial correlations. Strong symmetry then promotes these correlations to the quantum domain, enabling global multipartite entanglement. Within weak-coupling theory, we obtain exact steady states despite the generator's nonquadratic nature: strong symmetry reduces their construction to a classical problem for arbitrary Ising couplings. This reduction reveals an exact connection between classical distinguishability and entanglement. We then show how to engineer the bath spectrum to increase the correlation length and enable the preparation of GHZ-like states from separable initial conditions. We test the mechanism beyond the analytical regime using exact Markovian embeddings and tensor-network simulations. Our approach is particularly suited to superconducting and trapped-ion platforms, and we propose a concrete implementation for the latter using sympathetically cooled motional modes.

quantum-devices.title: Quantum Gate Engineering in Superconducting NISQ Platforms: Experimental Methods and Emerging Directions
quantum-devices.summary: This review aims to provide researchers, experimentalists, and quantum engineers with an updated and technically grounded perspective on the implementation of quantum gates in superconducting NISQ devices. The goal is to establish a comprehensive bridge between theoretical quantum circuit synthesis and its practical, experimental implementation, focusing on superconducting quantum technologies. We systematically examine the diverse landscape of superconducting qubits and processor architectures, ranging from conventional transmons to alternative and unconventional designs, evaluating their unique design trade-offs, connectivity constraints, device physics, and materials impact. Moving from theory to actual implementation, we detail how single- and two-qubit operations are synthesized via microwave-driven and flux-activated pulses. We here present our pulse engineering, wave shaping, calibration workflows, demonstrating how to bridge the gap between abstract gate models and real-world hardware limitations in the direction of a hardware-software co-design framework. To validate these operations, we choose benchmarking methodologies with the purpose to get the more efficient metric for the specific evaluation aspect, including truth tables and quantum process tomography. Therefore, we both discuss the theoretical concepts behind the gate synthesis and show experimental implementation of most fundamental gates by proposing a practical workflow.

quantum-devices.title: Pulse-Informed Physical Placement for Parallel Two-Qubit Gates in Qubit Arrays
quantum-devices.summary: A parallel two-qubit layer can often be realized with several nonoverlapping sets of physical couplers, but isolated calibrations do not reveal how each realization performs after optimizing its own simultaneous control pulse. We formulate physical placement and pulse synthesis as a coupled decision problem for parallel controlled-$Z$ gates in heterogeneous frequency tunable transmon arrays. The proposed processor-aware structural quantum multi-domain matrix (QMDM) links static processor, edge, incidence, and task information to a dynamic candidate response block. For each candidate placement $P$, QMDM instantiates the active Hamiltonian $H_P$; quantum optimal control (QOCT) generates a placement-specific pulse, direct coupled propagation returns the projected computational subspace overlap $F_{\rm proj}$ and computational survival; and these pulse-conditioned responses are fed back to QMDM to rank and progressively promote physical placements. This placement pulse response feedback defines pulse-informed physical placement. Here, to see the performance of the proposed method on 30 held-out synthetic $3\times3$ processors, the median final $F_{\rm proj}$ is $0.993826$ for pulse-informed placement and $0.984981$ for calibration-based placement. Also, when tested under different system conditions, the proposed pulse-informed approach uses $59.1\%$ fewer candidate QOCT optimizer iterations than the exhaustive finite-budget reference. The QMDM representation and outer search are formulated for arbitrary $L$ simultaneous two-qubit gates. Here, the present global candidate ranking validation is used for $L=2$.

quantum-devices.title: Maximally-Matched Mixture Decoding for Correlated Atom Loss in Quantum LDPC Codes
quantum-devices.summary: Heralded atom loss is a dominant noise channel in neutral atom quantum computing platforms, and losses at a two-qubit gate are strongly correlated: when one atom is lost, its gate partner is often lost too. This work shows how to exploit this correlation to construct a better decoder, focusing on [[144,12,12]] Gross code syndrome extraction circuits. Given a loss readout, the possible pairings of the lost qubits according to shared gates form a graph whose maximum matchings carry almost all of the conditional probability mass. Our maximal-matching-mixture (MMM) decoder builds a per-readout decoding hypergraph as a weighted mixture over exactly these loss scenarios. This decoding hypergraph can be used by an ordinary belief-propagation decoder. On the [[144,12,12]] Gross code, MMM lowers the logical error rate by as much as ~25x relative to a loss-unaware decoder and ~2x relative to a loss-aware uniform-mixture baseline from Baranes et al. (2026).

quantum-devices.title: Optimal quantum discrimination at Liouvillian exceptional points
quantum-devices.summary: Central to non-Hermitian sensing is the question of whether exceptional points (EPs) can make weak perturbations easier to detect. We show that despite enhanced spectral response, in finite-dimensional Lindblad systems with a unique stationary state and a nonzero relaxation gap, EPs offer no fundamental advantage in how the observation time required for reliable detection of a weak perturbation scales with the perturbation strength. We nevertheless demonstrate that by selectively choosing perturbations that enhance the quantum Fisher information rate, EPs can shorten the observation time needed to reach a predefined detection accuracy relative to a comparable non-EP reference at the same decay rate. As an illustration, we show using an optomechanical model at an EP that we can detect a weak force through the cavity output at the same reliability in less time than a non-EP reference. Our results establish fundamental limits on perturbation detection at EPs and can guide the design of faster non-Hermitian sensors based on optomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, and trapped ions.

quantum-devices.title: Quantum Evolution Kernel for Node-Attributed Graphs
quantum-devices.summary: We present a novel approach to embed node-attributed graphs onto neutral-atom quantum computers, and propose an application to digit recognition. Our approach extends PASQAL's quantum evolution kernel (QEK) by introducing a node-level feature encoding based on three-level quantum states. To this purpose, we present a prototype showing how the resulting embedding can be leveraged to extract correlation-based information for classification tasks. The entire quantum process is simulated using Pasqal's Pulser library, which inevitably imposes constraints on the size of the experimental datasets. We compare our method with classical baselines to evaluate its potential. We show that, for the digit recognition task, our method achieves a higher mean accuracy than the more commonly used Jensen-Shannon distance-based methods by utilizing the Wasserstein distance.

quantum-devices.title: From QCCD Trapped-Ion Hardware to Quantum Compilers: Capabilities, Architectures, and Compilation
quantum-devices.summary: Shuttling-based trapped-ion quantum computers (QCCD) rank among the most mature hardware platforms. Existing and envisaged devices exhibit architectural differences in terms of register layout and connectivity. Platform-specific compilers are required to translate quantum circuits into resource-optimized hardware-level command chains. Hardware platforms and compiler software stacks are mostly developed independently of one another by different research communities. This work aims to bridge these communities by abstracting QCCD architectures and native operations, enabling computer scientists to address compilation problems using generic methods without requiring a deep background in the physical operating principles of the platform. The resulting design space is organized into a small set of architectural archetypes, each posing its own compilation problem. We then select and apply compilation methods to one- and two-dimensional QCCD architectures, finding that the routing overhead scales approximately cubically with the number of qubits for the one-dimensional architecture and approximately quadratically for the two-dimensional one. Extending this to compilation with a quantum error-correction layer reveals additional differences and similarities between the physical and logical levels. We conclude that co-design is a requirement rather than an option, and this work provides the vocabulary, archetypes, and compilation abstraction it needs.

quantum-devices.title: Correlation-sensitive magic-state distillation from spin-squeezed neutral atoms
quantum-devices.summary: We show that interblock correlations can reverse magic-state distillation even when every input exceeds the threshold for independent states. For the five-to-one Bravyi-Kitaev protocol with independent local Clifford twirls, we express the output in terms of measurable target-axis moments. Fourth-order correlations determine acceptance, while third- and fifth-order correlations determine the output polarization. This relation yields a direct sign test for distillation gain and opposite gains for inputs with identical single-qubit and two-qubit reduced states. We connect this mechanism to neutral-atom resource preparation through finite-range Ising dynamics. Block separation suppresses detrimental interblock coupling, and locally addressed Clifford phases release interaction-generated magic from a spin-squeezed precursor by changing the symmetry selected by code projection. A protocol that retains accepted source outputs achieves positive gain above a source-contrast threshold set by circuit errors and storage dephasing. The same moments specify a finite-sample experimental diagnostic. These results connect the correlation structure of a resource state to its preparation, acceptance, and distillation gain.

quantum-devices.title: Qubit-environment entanglement in pure dephasing dynamics for mixed initial states
quantum-devices.summary: Decoherence of qubits is one main limitation in quantum information processing, where the qubits themselves can be mixed because of decoherence and additional decoherence may generated through interactions with a bath. Here, we present a complete study of qubit-environment entanglement in the case of interactions that lead to pure dephasing of the qubit by allowing the initial state of the qubit to be mixed, exceeding previous restrictions. We find that the criteria for separability that hold for pure initial states of the qubit are reduced to witness status. Yet, the evolution of the witnesses reflects the array of features that entanglement can exhibit in the mixed case but are forbidden in the pure-qubit case. Most notably, this includes sudden birth of entanglement as the initial phase of the evolution is typically separable. Moreover, there is a stark numerical advantage to the study of entanglement for large environments when using the witness rather than the traditional measures available. We include the study of entanglement generated between a spin qubit and a sparse spin environment to illustrate the peculiarities of the evolution of entanglement in this case, as well as to emphasize the level of reliability of the entanglement witness.

quantum-devices.title: Finite-temperature Quantum Quasinormal Mode Theory for Spatiotemporally-resolved Dissipative Cavity Quantum Magnonics
quantum-devices.summary: Cavity quantum magnonics has ushered in an unprecedented era of hybrid light-matter interfaces in which microwave photons, collective spin excitations, and superconducting or spin qubits can be coupled within a single device architecture, facilitating a versatile platform for quantum information processing. Realizing their full potential, however, requires a theory that can treat non-reciprocal magnetic media, material dissipation and open-cavity radiation losses, as well as finite-temperature fluctuations rigorously and without significant approximation. The dissipative magnonic resonances of such systems are described as quasinormal modes (QNMs), yet a consistent quantization procedure for lossy gyrotropic resonators has remained elusive. In this work, we present a finite-temperature quantum QNM theory, based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media and complex coordinate transformations, that achieves QNM quantization for a wide class of spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative and dispersive, cavity magnonic systems. We demonstrate the predictive capabilities of our theory via applications to hybrid dielectric-magnonic resonators interacting with both spin and superconducting qubits, evidencing modal interference effects, a continuous transition from coherent to dissipative coupling, spatiotemporal quantum field dynamics, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization, at both zero and finite temperatures. By addressing the intricacies of modal loss and non-reciprocity in a fully quantum theory of cavity magnonics, our approach enables the quantitative design of hybrid quantum devices that operate under realistic open-system and thermal conditions, without recourse to ad hoc quantization schemes.

quantum-devices.title: Suppressing microwave crosstalk in superconducting quantum processors by designing parasitic drive capacitances
quantum-devices.summary: As superconducting quantum processors scale to large qubit counts, unwanted microwave drive crosstalk becomes an important source of coherent errors. Here, we investigate the role of parasitic coupling paths in the suppression of drive crosstalk in a processor with two fixed-frequency transmon qubits and a tunable coupler. To account for the many different coupling paths, we develop a detailed circuit model to capture the dependence of crosstalk on the coupler frequency. We experimentally demonstrate suppression of crosstalk, finding that the suppression does not originate solely from cancellation of the effective qubit-qubit coupling, but also is a result of interference between other coupling paths. Building on these insights, we show that drive crosstalk can be suppressed with the right choice of parasitic capacitances, which otherwise often are treated as unwanted design imperfections. Our results provide practical guidance for low-crosstalk device design of superconducting quantum processors and point toward a broader strategy in which parasitic coupling paths are engineered rather than simply minimized.

quantum-devices.title: Analog Quantum Experiments Meet Automatic Differentiation - from Programs to Atoms
quantum-devices.summary: Gradient-based optimization of analog quantum hardware poses a concrete programming problem: given an executable experiment P(θ) that returns only measurement samples, what executable experiment should the system run to obtain (d/dθ_ell)P(θ)? Conventional automatic differentiation cannot propagate through the inaccessible quantum state, while finite differences require a noise-sensitive step size and analytic gradient identities cover only parts of an experiment. We present DiffSimuQ, which shows that a broad class of open-loop analog quantum experiments is closed under automatic differentiation. A compositional transformation maps P(θ) to a derivative program D_ell[P(θ)] in the same language whose expected outcome is exactly the derivative. Only continuous evolution requires a strategy-specific rule, and we give two realizations. Our Nyquist shift rule (NSR) applies to general time-dependent evolution: we prove that the observable response to shifting the Hamiltonian along its tangent is band-limited even for non-commuting controls, enabling exact reconstruction from shifted executions. For involutory generators, a parameter-shift realization (PSR) inserts a parameter-independent operation at a sampled time. Because derivative programs remain ordinary programs, source and derivative experiments share one compiler, which reuses the source realization, lowers branches to device-ready neutral-atom controls, and selects between NSR and PSR based on estimated cost. Under device noise, the exact derivative programs differentiate the objective realized by the device, with hardware realization errors treated separately. In machine-level noisy emulation, NSR and PSR avoid the finite-difference error floor and improve closed-loop optimization; they win in complementary cost regimes, while each derivative branch at 1000 qubits add at most 0.3% to source compilation time.

quantum-devices.title: Bargmann-invariant witness of the graviton commutator
quantum-devices.summary: We identify the phase of a Bargmann invariant of two matter-wave interferometers as a quantum gravity signature that cannot be reproduced by any branchwise-definite classical gravitational field. For matter coupled linearly to linearized gravity, the interferometric coherence factorizes exactly into a conservative Newtonian phase, the characteristic functional of the graviton state, and a commutator phase. For Wigner-positive graviton states, the first two are classically reproducible; therefore, decoherence alone cannot certify that gravity is quantized. The Bargmann phase isolates the commutator, which is independent of the graviton state and of all Newtonian interactions and is bounded by which-path decoherence. For gravity, this radiation-reaction effect is sixty orders of magnitude below experimental reach, but trapped-ion analogs can test it at order unity.

quantum-devices.title: Neutrinos as Quantum Information Carriers? A Gap Analysis Against the DiVincenzo Criteria
quantum-devices.summary: Photons, trapped ions, neutral atoms, and superconducting circuits are all well-known quantum information platforms. Neutrinos offer a unique possibility, displaying quantum interference (flavour oscillation) over thousands of kilometres, yet interacting so weakly that they can travel through the Earth with minimal interaction. This short paper is a gap analysis. We use information from the existing literature to compare neutrinos to the seven DiVincenzo requirements. Firstly, there are five requirements to do with computation and secondly two requirements to do with communication. We analyse where the gaps are for each requirement. Overall, we find that neutrinos have high fidelity and good coherence; however, they do not have a clear qubit definition and initialisation. They do not have universal gates, individual qubit readout, or stationary-to-flying conversion, meaning they either fail or are very poor. Therefore, we think they are best considered as an exceptional flying information carrier; however, they are very difficult to control. We have outlined all of the gaps which can be used to inform future work.

quantum-devices.title: Real-Time Correlation of Relaxation, Dephasing, and Two-level System Dynamics in Transmon Qubits
quantum-devices.summary: Materials improvements in transmon qubits have yielded remarkable advances in qubit lifetimes (T1)and coherence times (T2). However, state-of-the-art superconducting qubits experience temporal fluctuations in their performance, which limit gate fidelities and quantum processor performance. We observe correlated increases in qubit relaxation and dephasing rates that last for minutes to hours, which we call T1 and T2 excursions. Using interleaved lifetime and coherence time measurements, noise spectroscopy, and two-level-system (TLS) spectroscopy, we find that these excursions are caused by single or few strongly-coupled TLS defects that spectrally diffuse into resonance with the qubit frequency. Our measurement protocol provides a powerful tool for understanding the noise sources that cause temporal fluctuations in superconducting qubit performance.

quantum-devices.title: When is a bosonic operator a Hamiltonian?
quantum-devices.summary: Hermitian polynomials in the quadrature operators $x$ and $p$ are the basic ingredients of continuous-variable quantum information, and increasingly exotic ones are now routinely engineered in superconducting circuits and trapped ions. However, such a polynomial need not define unique quantum dynamics: it may define exactly one, none, or an infinite family of physically distinct ones. Such obstructions are invisible to algebraic arguments and can compromise finite-dimensional truncations, which may fail to converge or silently converge to the wrong dynamics. We develop a method, implemented as an algorithm, which decides which case occurs, and how large the family is, from the coefficients alone, with no functional-analytic input from the user. For Gaussian operators the answer is always one; for non-Gaussian ones, a regime continuous-variable quantum computing cannot do without, the other outcomes occur already for simple and physically natural Hamiltonians. We apply the algorithm to operators drawn from the recent literature.

quantum-devices.title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
quantum-devices.summary: Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

quantum-devices.title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
quantum-devices.summary: We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using \texttt{ibm\_phoenix}, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to $\sim 2\cdot 10^{-7}$ over 170 measurement rounds.

quantum-devices.title: Demonstrating RFSoC-based Control of a Fully Connected Exchange-Only Qubit
quantum-devices.summary: Semiconductor triple-quantum dots (TQDs) are a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, but the community has so far lacked access to affordable and flexible high-speed control electronics. SpinQICK, an open-source spin qubit-control package built on the Xilinx Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC), directly addresses this gap by leveraging the high sampling-rate signal generation and advanced digital signal processing (DSP) capabilities of the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) to enable precise time-domain voltage control and readout of semiconductor spin qubits. In this paper, we use spinQICK to demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only device. We also introduce and experimentally verify a novel dynamical decoupling (DD) sequence enabled by the triangular TQD and leverage its unique decoupling properties to characterize electrical noise. These results establish spinQICK as a low-cost, flexible platform for semiconductor spin qubit control and provide a pathway for hardware optimization through qubit-level noise diagnostics.

quantum-devices.title: Optimal Control of a Fluxonium Circuit with the Q-PRONTO Numerical Method
quantum-devices.summary: Optimizing the control of large quantum systems is a resource-intensive task, where the convergence rate of the underlying iterative schemes is crucial. The recently developed Quantum Projection Operator-Based Newton Method for Trajectory Optimization (Q-PRONTO) offers a unique quadratic convergence for controlling quantum states, while most model-based solvers guarantee only an approximately linear convergence rate. As a proof of concept, here, we design and benchmark single-qubit gates optimized by Q-PRONTO based on the circuit Hamiltonian of a fluxonium superconducting qubit. To ensure that we can apply a long string of arbitrary pulses to the circuit, we modify the firmware associated with the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) by altering its memory allocation. We characterize the performance of the optimal solutions using standard randomized benchmarking and achieve a total error per gate of $6.6\times10^{-4}$.

quantum-devices.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. II. System-parameter uncertainties and overall errors
quantum-devices.summary: In the companion paper (Part I), we developed an optimal-control framework to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors in controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons. Here, we extend this framework to incorporate uncertainties in coupling strength, anharmonicities, and zero-flux qubit frequencies, enabling the design of high-fidelity gates robust against noise and parameter uncertainties. We classify these uncertainties by whether they perturb the off-diagonal coupling strengths or the diagonal detunings of the Hamiltonian, and we identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated through dynamical decoupling induced by strong detuning modulation. For a 30-ns gate, this strategy reduces the coupling error to $6.21\times10^{-7}$ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to $2π\times4$ MHz while keeping total gate infidelity below $10^{-3}$. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances the two dominant leakage-mediated interactions. A 24-ns gate operated near this point tolerates individual uncertainties of up to $2π\times5$ MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. We further optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance. The resulting stage-specific controls achieve lower infidelity and greater robustness. Together with the companion study (Part I), this framework offers a practical approach to balance speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

quantum-devices.title: Mode-Selective Micromotion Compensation via Coherent Excitation of a Ground-State-Cooled Motional Mode
quantum-devices.summary: Excess micromotion induced by stray DC electric fields limits the control fidelity of trapped-ion experiments. Various techniques have been developed to detect and compensate ion displacements from the RF null by monitoring modulated fluorescence, ion positions, or micromotion sidebands. Although these approaches are effective, they do not probe the displacement through a ground-state-cooled motional mode and therefore offer limited compatibility with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols. Here, we demonstrate a micromotion compensation method based on the driven coherent amplitude of a ground-state-cooled motional mode. In this approach, the ion displacement is converted into a coherent motional excitation by an auxiliary RF drive and detected through the qubit. We determine the optimal compensation field with a $1σ$ statistical uncertainty of 8 mV/m. The method is naturally compatible with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols employing nonclassical motional states, including Fock, squeezed, and Schrödinger-cat states, providing a pathway toward quantum-enhanced micromotion compensation.

quantum-devices.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
quantum-devices.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

quantum-devices.title: Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors
quantum-devices.summary: Modular quantum architecture requires long-distance quantum interconnects to stitch together individual processor modules. Such interconnects, long-distance couplers or L-couplers, must support coherent quantum operation over meter-scale distances and scale to multiple connections between any two modules. Here we demonstrate four L-couplers operating between two 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting qubit processors. Each L-coupler joins two Nighthawk lattice qubits through two frequency-tunable L-qubits, two RF-SQUID based "i2m" couplers, and 80 cm of superconducting aluminum coax. Each cable installs perpendicular to the processor surface, to enable denser connections, and is joined to the chip by an indium-to-indium room temperature pressure bond made after both modules were mounted. L-coupler modes near 5 GHz, with internal quality factors of 0.86 to 1.09e6, carry relay-based state transfer at a mean network benchmarking fidelity of 99.00%, with a best link of 99.29 +/- 0.07%. We then realize distant CZ gates between lattice qubits in separate modules at a mean fidelity of 94.75%, with a best link of 96.42 +/- 0.28%, and use them to generate entangled states across the two processors, including a demonstration of simultaneous Bell pair generation using two adjacent L-couplers. These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing.
quantum-devices.comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 1 table, plus Extended Data

quantum-devices.title: Encoding a bosonic mode into qubits for simulating boson-matter interactions
quantum-devices.summary: We explore the space-time cost of encoding of a bosonic mode into a set of qubits via various encodings, and their resilience to noise. In particular, we compare the performance of the unary Fock state encoding, an unexplored encoding of Fock states into Dicke states (``Dicke'' encoding), and the binary quadrature encoding. We do so by considering a displacement as well as a simulation of a Dicke model, coupling a bosonic mode to a set of atoms represented as qubits. Using classical simulations, we assess the accuracy and optimized space-time costs in terms of number of qubits, circuit depth and CNOT count of a quantum simulation of the time dynamics using these encodings. Although our study is far from comprehensive, we find that the binary quadrature encoding is overall most favorable in terms of being very space-efficient and relatively time-efficient due to the use of the quantum Fourier transform. Our novel Dicke encoding leads to very shallow circuits, but pays in terms of using many more qubits. We probe the use of an H2-2 Quantinuum trapped-ion qubit device (56 qubits) for displacement and Dicke model simulation in the low boson-number regime, where we find that noise leads to visible deviations from ideal circuit dynamics.

quantum-devices.title: Semiclassical molecular dynamics simulations of electromagnetically induced transparency cooling of 2D and 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap
quantum-devices.summary: Motional modes of trapped-ion crystals in Penning traps can now be cooled to near their ground states via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) cooling. Numerical simulations are valuable tools for interpreting EIT cooling results and optimizing experimental protocols, but existing molecular dynamics codes are limited to the simulation of Doppler cooling. In this work, we fill this gap by implementing a semiclassical model of EIT cooling in a novel MD code. By simultaneously evolving the ions' internal quantum states and classical motion, we are able to calculate the instantaneous EIT laser forces acting on the ions. We first validate our code by comparing the single-ion cooling rate to fully quantum simulation results. Next, we analyze cooling of the drumhead modes in planar ion crystals, quantifying the effects of planar ion motion and a finite laser beam width. Finally, we demonstrate efficient EIT cooling of the axial modes in 3D ellipsoidal crystals containing up to 500 ions. Such crystals are a promising platform for future quantum sensing experiments with enhanced sensitivity. We find that the mode spectra of 3D crystals can be engineered to enable sympathetic cooling of the low-frequency $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ modes. This numerical framework provides a powerful tool for modeling sub-Doppler cooling techniques and for optimizing future quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.

quantum-devices.title: NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
quantum-devices.summary: Quantum low-density parity-check codes now reach encoding rates up to 50% at useful distances. Their checks however are long-range group actions, not local neighbourhoods, and that connectivity has so far been supplied by neutral atoms. Silicon spin qubits offer the same primitive --- coherent transport of qubit blocks --- through electron shuttling, and on microsecond rather than millisecond timescales. They however travel along fabricated tracks rather than free space: permutations an atom array obtains by moving tweezers must here become collision-free motions on a physical lattice. We here present the first code and spin-qubit hardware co-design. We build an architecture whose geometry mimics that of a family of non-abelian groups, broad enough to host codes of excellent parameters: a hierarchy of nested conveyor-belt loops on a plain square lattice of shuttling tracks, in which every group multiplication becomes a rigid, globally controlled motion of whole qubit trains. We call it NeST, for Nested Shuttling Tracks. A code search over the family returns rate-20% mitten codes up to $[[1400,280,\leq 28]]$, and circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing give thresholds above $10^{-3}$ with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles, two to three orders of magnitude faster than neutral-atom implementations. Via extrapolations, we estimate that this largest code may reach a logical error probability per qubit per round of $10^{-14}$, assuming a ten-fold improvement on early shuttling demonstrations, with other physical errors at p=0.1%. Logic is compatible with NeST too: for the [[150,30,10]] code we build a code-surgery gadget in which every qubit again moves only by rigid belt motions, at no qubit cost and a 29% increase in gate layers. This demonstrates that ultra-low-overhead fault tolerance and a fast clock speed are not competing goals, and that silicon spin qubits can supply both.

quantum-devices.title: Tuning between collective dynamics and scrambling through initial-state symmetry alignment in long-range spin models
quantum-devices.summary: Long-range interactions in many-body quantum systems give rise to a wide range of dynamical phenomena, from collective dynamics well described by integrable mean-field models with symmetric all-to-all couplings, to fast scrambling of quantum information from disordered long-range interactions. Here, we investigate scenarios in which both regimes emerge within a single deterministic, translation-invariant XY spin model with long-range couplings. We consider a sparse powers-of-two (PWR2) graph, where each spin interacts with a logarithmic number of neighbors, and a power-law-decaying model. By altering the initial state via local perturbations on a completely symmetric state, we show that the dynamics changes from collective to scrambling as witnessed by bipartite and multipartite entanglement measures. We characterize this collective-to-scrambling crossover using Lyapunov exponents in the semiclassical regime, and show that the spectral properties of the coupling graph adjacency matrix provide a very efficient tool to predict the onset of fast scrambling. Our results offer a unified framework for controlling the switch between collective and scrambling dynamics in a setup accessible in experiments with neutral atoms in cavities or in tweezer arrays.
quantum-devices.comment: 20 pages, 11 figures in the main text, and 6 figures in the appendices

quantum-devices.title: Quantum Simulation of the Static Yukawa Model via Effective Particles on a Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulator
quantum-devices.summary: Trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and circuit QED quantum computers naturally enable coupled qubit-boson simulations. Boson-fermion interactions arise in quantum field theory, where renormalization is required to obtain finite results. We study one of the simplest examples of a coupled fermion-boson system, the static Yukawa model, on the QSCOUT trapped-ion system. We use similarity renormalization to express the same physics in terms of effective particles described by different values of the renormalization parameter $s$. This enables us to map data taken in the window of bosonic occupancy that is experimentally accessible to larger occupancies of distinct effective particles. We use this to study strongly coupled, high-occupancy regimes despite limited readout ranges. Using a trapped-ion qubit-boson device on Sandia National Laboratories' QSCOUT platform, we demonstrate the time evolution of the static Yukawa model.

quantum-devices.title: Structured light for addressable two-qubit gates in medium-sized ion crystals: modeling motional and dephasing errors
quantum-devices.summary: Geometric phase gates with addressed laser radiation are widely used in trapped-ion quantum computers to drive high-fidelity entangling gates on an arbitrary qubit pair of a larger ion chain. Such programmable connectivity exploits the collective phonons to mediate the desired interaction, while simultaneously achieving robustness to their thermal fluctuations by a careful calibration of the gate time with respect to the laser and vibrational-mode frequencies. Crosstalk errors can arise when the spectator qubits, which should ideally remain idle during the gate, are partially driven by the laser fields. The minimal crosstalk, which is set by the laser beam size on the spectator ions, can be achieved when the addressing beams propagate perpendicular to the ion chain. However, this results in exciting the radial phonons, and can complicate achieving high-fidelities as the ion chain grows due to the so-called spectral mode crowding. In this work, we present the theoretical description of a scheme recently implemented by Faorlin et $al.$. This scheme overcomes these complications by engineering addressable state-dependent forces along the ion-chain with laser beams that propagate perpendicular to it through the use of structured light gradients. In this way, one can excite the axial phonons and avoid the spectral mode crowding, while simultaneously minimizing the crosstalk. We present a detailed derivation of the entangling gate scheme, together with analytical closed-form expressions for the leading contribution to the gate error caused by thermal motional fluctuations and dephasing noise. Our results confirm that such fluctuations account for up to 93$\%$ of the error budget under the operating conditions of the gate implemented by Faorlin et $al.$. We identify target parameters to reduce the motional error from the reported $10^{-3}$ to the $10^{-5}$ level.

quantum-devices.title: Phase shifts and fluctuations from motional, relativistic, and dark-matter effects in ion-trap clocks
quantum-devices.summary: Ions possess both center-of-mass motion and internal states, rendering trapped-ion optical clocks susceptible to perturbations of both degrees of freedom, which results in systematic shifts and fluctuations with motional and relativistic origins. We develop a quantum theory that connects these effects to filter functions determined by the employed pulse sequences and show how the interrogation can be tailored to suppress or enhance specific perturbations. Our treatment includes laser frequency noise and motional effects such as recoil and Doppler shifts, micromotion and excess micromotion, as well as state-dependent trap imperfections and accelerations, e.g., caused by Stark shifts. We further account for relativistic effects including time dilation and the mass defect, and show how the same framework can be applied to hypothetical dark-matter signals. By considering ensemble-averaged phases and their variances, we characterize both systematic shifts and fluctuations, while asynchronous operation relative to the Paul-trap drive allows motional fluctuations to average down between runs. Our results provide a unified framework for characterizing and controlling the systematic and statistical contributions that determine the trueness and precision of trapped-ion optical clocks.

quantum-devices.title: Trapped-ion-based quantum repeater node across a 17 km metropolitan fiber
quantum-devices.summary: Concatenation of quantum repeater nodes has been proposed as a means to distribute entanglement efficiently across future long-distance networks. Here, we demonstrate a trapped-ion repeater node that establishes photonic entanglement over a 17 km fiber traversing a city, moving beyond laboratory-only prototypes. The node comprises two atomic ions coupled to an optical cavity. First, a detailed characterization is performed of the long fiber channel and of ion-photon entanglement distributed across it. Next, a repeater-node protocol is implemented, achieving entanglement between a local photon and a remote photon with a Bell-state fidelity of $81.6^{+1.9}_{-1.4}\%$. These results demonstrate that trapped-ion repeater-node technology can operate over existing city-scale fiber infrastructure and represent a step toward distributed quantum repeater networks.

quantum-devices.title: Controlled-Z Gates via Floquet Coupling to Two Auxiliary States in Transmon Circuits
quantum-devices.summary: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for quantum information processing. In transmon circuits, higher excited states provide additional pathways for engineering interactions within the computational subspace. Here we demonstrate controlled-Z (CZ) gates that exploit two noncomputational states, $\ket{02}$ and $\ket{20}$, through selective Floquet coupling. The nontrivial parametric modulation can activate both auxiliary transitions from $\ket{11}$ while suppressing the leading exchange between $\ket{01}$ and $\ket{10}$. Based on this approach, we develop two gate protocols: a nonadiabatic round trip through a bright auxiliary superposition and adiabatic evolution along a zero-energy dark state, both achieving average gate fidelities above $99.99\%$ in numerical simulations. Control of the modulation phase further extends the bright-state protocol to conventional and unconventional geometric CZ gates. Effective-model simulations show that unconventional control improves tolerance to residual $ZZ$ coupling and static qubit-frequency offsets relative to conventional control over the parameter ranges examined. Simulations including neighboring spectator qubits show that the original nonadiabatic bright-state and adiabatic dark-state CZ protocols retain high gate fidelities. This framework offers new routes toward the experimental realization of CZ gates and their geometric implementations.

quantum-devices.title: Multimode Parametric Amplifier for K-Band Quantum Measurements
quantum-devices.summary: We demonstrate K-band nondegenerate three-wave-mixing amplification in a multimode resonator comprising an array of 500 SNAILs. Pairing K-band signal modes with lower-frequency internal idler modes enables 20 dB of gain continuously from 19.6 to 25.6 GHz with pump frequencies below 32.2 GHz. At 20 dB gain, the 3-dB bandwidth ranges from 2.6 to 11.7 MHz, and the input-referred 1-dB compression power reaches -100.9 dBm. In the 20-22 GHz band, the average added noise is 0.73 quanta. A two-mode nondegenerate parametric amplification model describes the measured gain response and gain-bandwidth behavior, while a multimode Kerr model captures the overall compression scale. Our amplifier provides a practical solution for implementing a state-of-the-art readout of superconducting qubits in the K-band.
quantum-devices.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; 3 pages of supplementary material

quantum-devices.title: Engineering \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions between two remote superconducting qubits via a multimode waveguide
quantum-devices.summary: Waveguides provide a flexible platform for long-range interactions between superconducting qubits. Here, we study how to engineer the effective \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions between two qubits via qubit frequency assignments and multimode interference determined by the mode configuration and standing-wave parities of a finite multimode waveguide. For a single-mode waveguide, we find that \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions cannot be simultaneously suppressed to zero and the residual qubit-qubit coupling always exists. For example, the \(XY\) interaction may be suppressed to a negligible level when two qubits and the waveguide mode satisfy the two-photon resonant condition, but the \(ZZ\) interaction cannot be switched off. For multimode configurations within the central dispersive window, the engineered interaction types are very different for odd and even numbers of modes. Even-mode configurations can readily produce strong \(XY\) interactions, whereas odd-mode configurations can strongly suppress the \(XY\) interaction while retaining a finite \(ZZ\) interaction. Full-Hamiltonian simulations of minimal two- and three-mode configurations confirm \(XY\)-dominated SWAP dynamics and \(ZZ\)-dominated CZ-type dynamics, respectively. These results establish a frequency assignment criterion of qubits and waveguide modes for selectively engineering long-range qubit-qubit interaction types induced by the waveguide with finite multimode.

quantum-devices.title: Active isolation of transmon readout with a tunable inductive bridge
